title: uks moron premium predates morons 2026 09 01
author: Jon Sindreu
text:
LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Ever since Prime Minister Liz Truss's disastrous mini-budget in 2022, Britain's persistently elevated borrowing costs have been attributed to what TS Lombard economist Dario Perkins jokingly dubbed the "moron risk premium". Cycling through three leaders since then has done little to challenge that diagnosis. Yet paradoxically, the gilt market's travails probably have less to do with the imprudence of prime ministers and more ​with how smart technocrats at the Debt Management Office (DMO) and the Bank of England (BoE) have handled the bonds.
Fixed-income assets have been pummeled over the past month. Investors' focus has largely been on the ‌United States, where Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has willingly created uncertainty about future monetary policy and the Treasury is trying to offset the damage by repurchasing more of its own long-maturity paper.
Yet U.S. 10-year bond yields are still below those of the United Kingdom, which exceed 5%. In France and Italy, they are roughly 4%. Thirty-year gilts, sensitive to political headlines, are trading at a steep 5.8%. It's a headache for British finance minister John Healey.
On the surface, it's unclear why investors single out the UK. France runs a budget deficit equal to 5.1% of ​GDP and Italy carries debt of 137% of GDP. Britain, by contrast, expects a 3.6% deficit this fiscal year with debt near 95% of output.
But the UK is an outlier in how it finances itself. Roughly 24% ​of its outstanding government bonds are inflation-linked, meaning their principal rises in line with the Retail Prices Index, versus 9% in France. Britain's debt also has an unusual average maturity ⁠of 14 years, nearly twice that of France, Italy and even Japan.
In an era of inflationary supply shocks and investor aversion to long lock-ups, these funding choices are themselves a huge liability. Historically, the DMO catered to the UK's massive "defined ​benefit" pension fund industry and its need to offset long-dated, inflation-indexed commitments with matching assets. But aging demographics and higher rates have prompted a shift towards plans that no longer promise a set amount to beneficiaries, causing an exodus from bonds, especially ​inflation-linked ones.
Until recently, the BoE was buying some of this paper. Now, it has become the only major central bank actively selling bonds, instead of just letting them mature. In September 2025, the BoE said it would reduce its £558 billion stash by £70 billion over a year, with £21 billion coming from outright sales.
Of course, with the BoE setting interest rates at 3.75%, compared with the ECB's 2.25%, it's hardly surprising UK long-term borrowing costs are higher.
Analysts therefore focus on the portion of yields that is unrelated to rate expectations, known as the "term premium," which explains ​why gilt yields kept rising after 2023 even as investors priced in interest rate cuts. This doesn't quite equate to the moron premium, since it reflects multiple forces, including global economic risks.
In its July staff report
, opens new tab
, the International Monetary Fund disentangled
, opens new tab
 these ​factors, building a statistical model that projects how different shocks affect the term premium. Risk specific to the UK, for example, should weaken the pound and widen the corporate-to-gilt spread. Researchers then compared those fingerprints to actual market moves.
Breakingviews replicated a similar model. Results vary ‌depending on the ⁠data source and shock duration, but show roughly the same pattern: UK-focused risk has crept in since the 2022 Truss fiasco, but the effect is modest. Global factors and a domestic supply-demand imbalance have had a much larger influence. The latter added a cumulative 60 basis points to 10-year yields since 2021.
Extending the statistical analysis further back, and comparing it to trends in Germany, is revealing. The numbers confirm that the DMO's strategy effectively involved trading much lower borrowing costs after 2016 - when ultra-low rates left pension funds desperate to plug funding gaps - for higher ones now. This reflects a structural shift, not political trauma: stable investors are rejecting the UK's debt mix, ceding the market to price-sensitive buyers. This includes hedge funds, which have ​ramped up their intermediation of rich-nation bonds.
It highlights a big flaw ​in traditional sovereign debt management, which counseled catering to ⁠existing investors and locking in the longest maturities during periods of low rates. The DMO wasn't alone: Austria and Ireland issued 100-year debt in 2017 and 2020. But the UK added to this a historical aversion to refinancing risk: short-dated Treasury bills make up only 3% of its debt stock, compared with 22% in the U.S. It also inherited a familiarity ​with perpetual bonds, and an unfortunate 1980s monetarist legacy
, opens new tab
 assuming inflation-linked debt would incentivise the government to prevent economic overheating.
Recent events exposed weaknesses in that logic. Modern sovereigns face less ​rollover risk than assumed, yet have ⁠limited inflation control and must often run persistent deficits to stabilise economies. A debt stock that becomes particularly unloved during energy-led inflation spikes creates greater problems than refinancing a larger share of liabilities at higher rates.
Indeed, many Western debt managers have been forced to tilt issuance toward shorter maturities, with the U.S Treasury's latest "Operation Twist" a stark example. Britain is no exception
, opens new tab
, cutting back on inflation-linked debt and reducing issuance of gilts of 20 years or more to near zero.
Given limited influence over the BoE, Healey should accelerate this ⁠shift when setting ​the DMO's annual financing remits
, opens new tab
. UK money market funds could become a powerful new source of demand for government debt, but have so far had ​scant bills to buy. The recent consultation
, opens new tab
 on expanding this market, which will lead to 12-month paper being issued, is a step in the right direction.
The U.S. is hardly an economic model to follow right now, and its attempts to swap long-term for short-term debt won't fix that. But minimising the ​bond volatility caused by the structure of the financial system, rather than actual fiscal policies, is still a worthy endeavour. Otherwise it's not just the politics that can get pretty moronic.
